before: Differentiation can happen right inside a family or a religion, and the same goes for a community or a relationship. You'd be belonging selectively, which still leaves room to belong. As a differentiated adult you can stay deeply embedded, free to question things or disagree, and if staying would mean disappearing, you're free to leave. If a parent used to go quiet and hurt whenever you disagreed, that might be hard to believe. A family where everyone gets to be their own person is healthier than an enmeshed one, and a faith that's your own is healthier than religious compliance. It can be the same religion either way. And two differentiated people have a sturdier relationship than two who've been absorbed into each other.
after: Differentiation is slow, and it goes on your whole life. If a family, group or relationship won't let you do this while you're still part of it, temporary distance may be necessary, and if they've actually hurt or threatened you, get safe first. Some people come back later on different terms. Sometimes the leaving is permanent, because going back would mean disappearing again, and you aren't punishing anyone by staying away. You don't have to know yet which one yours is. As you differentiate, you learn to tell the difference. Can they hear you disagree? If they can and you still disappear around them, that might just mean you're early in this.

guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
In ordinary life, the movement looks like this:

Other people’s emotions and opinions stop automatically replacing your own.

You notice when you agree in the moment and disagree later—and when praise, attraction, fear, or belonging suddenly changes what you think you know.

You can care about somebody’s feelings without sacrificing your own ground.

You can disappoint people, withstand social pressure, and remain recognizably yourself across settings.

You can love people in a family, religion, relationship, or political group without becoming the group identity, and question what you were programmed to believe while holding the discomfort.
brief:
- in ordinary life, the movement looks like this (every item of the guide's list; a sign isn't a test):
  - other people's emotions and opinions stop automatically replacing your own
  - you notice when you agree in the moment and disagree later (P3 of this h2 already says praise, pity, fear, attraction or resonance can suddenly change what you think you know, so don't repeat that half)
  - you can care about somebody's feelings without sacrificing your own ground
  - you can disappoint people, withstand social pressure, and stay recognizably yourself across settings (not identical everywhere)
  - you can love people in a family, religion, relationship or political group without becoming the group identity, and question what you were programmed to believe while holding the discomfort ("question", not reject)
- keep "automatically" and "notice": others' views can still change yours, and caring about their feelings stays
note: Turn 49 (2026-10-12): the h3's "In ordinary life, the movement looks like this:" and its list. Dedup: mostly partly said, as problems, not as signs; agreeing now and disagreeing later is new.
length: a short lead-in sentence, then the signs as a list, one per line, each starting with "- ", 70 to 120 words in all
